stem: A model `fct_reviews` has an enforced contract declaring five columns, each with a `data_type`. The model's SQL `select` statement returns those five columns plus one extra column that is not declared anywhere in the contract. The team needs to predict whether this model builds. What happens?

option_texts.A: The build succeeds, and the extra column is added to the warehouse table without a declared type
option_texts.B: The build succeeds, and dbt silently drops the undeclared extra column before loading it into the contract's table
option_texts.C: The build fails, because the preflight check requires the query's returned columns to match the contract's declared columns exactly
option_texts.D: The build succeeds, because contracts only restrict declared columns and ignore anything beyond that list

drill_answer_short: A preflight check compares the query's columns against the contract exactly; an extra column fails it
decision_hinge: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns with names and data types matching the ones you have defined, or it will fail to build.

plausible_options.D: plus one extra column that is not declared anywhere in the contract

A.signal: plus one extra column that is not declared anywhere in the contract
A.requires_fact: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns matching the ones you have defined, or it will fail to build.

eliminated_by.B: The team needs to predict whether this model builds

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — a contract requires every returned column to have a declared, matching data_type
distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — dbt does not silently drop extra columns to make a contracted query fit
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — a contract's guarantee covers the whole returned set, not only the declared subset

stem: A model `dim_listings_cleansed` declares an enforced contract with five columns in its YAML, including `listing_id` as `integer`. A recent SQL edit accidentally drops `listing_id` from the final `select` list, while the other four declared columns are still returned. The team needs to know what happens on the next build.

option_texts.A: dbt automatically re-adds `listing_id` by inferring it from the YAML definition
option_texts.B: The build succeeds, and `listing_id` is created as a `NULL`-only column to satisfy the declared contract
option_texts.C: The build succeeds, because contracts only check the columns a query does return, not ones it omits
option_texts.D: The build fails, because the preflight check requires every declared column to actually appear in the query's output

drill_answer_short: A declared contract column missing from the query output fails the preflight check
decision_hinge: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns with names and data types matching the ones you have defined, or it will fail to build.

plausible_options.C: A recent SQL edit accidentally drops `listing_id` from the final `select` list

A.signal: A recent SQL edit accidentally drops `listing_id` from the final `select` list
A.requires_fact: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns matching the ones you have defined, or it will fail to build.

eliminated_by.B: The team needs to know what happens on the next build

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — dbt has no mechanism to auto-insert a column a query forgot to select
distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — dbt does not synthesize a missing column out of nulls to satisfy a contract
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — the preflight check compares the full declared set, not just what the query happens to return

stem: `dim_listings_cleansed` defines `v: 1` and `v: 2`, with `latest_version: 2`. A downstream model needs to keep building against version 1 specifically, even after version 2 becomes the default. Which `ref()` call pins it to version 1?

option_texts.A: `ref('dim_listings_cleansed')`, since omitting the version always resolves to the oldest one
option_texts.C: `ref('dim_listings_cleansed_v1')`, treating the version suffix as part of the model's name
option_texts.D: `ref('dim_listings_cleansed', version='latest')`, since 'latest' always means the lowest version number

drill_answer_short: Pin a version explicitly with the v= argument to ref()
decision_hinge: ref('dim_customers', v=1) resolves to the database relation for that specific version, independent of which version is marked latest.

plausible_options.C: even after version 2 becomes the default

A.signal: even after version 2 becomes the default
A.requires_fact: If latest_version is not specified explicitly, the latest_version would be the numerically greatest version; an unversioned ref() resolves to the latest_version, not the oldest.

eliminated_by.D: even after version 2 becomes the default

distractor_traps.A: T4: breaks a stated fact — an unversioned ref() follows latest_version, which is explicitly set to 2 here, not the oldest
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — the versioned file may be named with a suffix, but ref() still takes the base model name plus a version argument
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — ref() has no `version='latest'` argument, and latest does not mean lowest

stem: A versioned model declares three versions, numbered 1 through 3, with `latest_version: 2` set explicitly. A reviewer needs to understand exactly what this `latest_version` property controls for downstream consumers. What is its purpose?

option_texts.A: It deletes every version other than the one specified once the project is built
option_texts.B: It determines which version number dbt treats as numerically highest for comparison purposes
option_texts.C: It determines which version an unversioned `ref()` call resolves to by default
option_texts.D: It determines the order in which versions are listed in the generated documentation site

drill_answer_short: latest_version sets which version an unversioned ref() call resolves to
decision_hinge: If latest_version is not specified explicitly, the latest_version would be the numerically greatest version. In this case, latest_version: 1 means v2 is a prerelease, in early development and testing.

plausible_options.B: declares three versions, numbered 1 through 3, with `latest_version: 2` set explicitly

eliminated_by.A: A reviewer needs to understand exactly what this `latest_version` property controls for downstream consumers
eliminated_by.D: A reviewer needs to understand exactly what this `latest_version` property controls for downstream consumers

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — older or newer versions keep building through their migration window, they are not deleted
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — latest_version overrides which version counts as latest, it does not change the numeric values themselves
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — documentation ordering is not what latest_version is documented to control

stem: Before opening a PR, a developer runs `dbt build --select +staging --empty`, and the entire build, models and tests included, succeeds in 30 seconds. The developer is ready to open the PR with confidence that the real data will build correctly too. Is that confidence justified by what `--empty` actually checked?

option_texts.A: Yes, because passing tests under `--empty` proves the same tests would pass against full production data
option_texts.B: Yes, because `--empty` still executes the model SQL against real data, just faster than a normal run
option_texts.C: No, because `--empty` does not connect to the warehouse at all, so nothing was actually validated
option_texts.D: No, because `--empty` limits refs and sources to zero rows, so it validates schema and dependencies but never touches real data values

drill_answer_short: --empty validates schema and dependencies with zero rows; it never touches real data values
decision_hinge: The --empty flag limits the refs and sources to zero rows. dbt will still execute the model SQL against the target data warehouse but will avoid expensive reads of input data. This validates dependencies and ensures your models will build properly.

plausible_options.A: the entire build, models and tests included, succeeds in 30 seconds

eliminated_by.B: the entire build, models and tests included, succeeds in 30 seconds

C.signal: the entire build, models and tests included, succeeds in 30 seconds
C.requires_fact: dbt will still execute the model SQL against the target data warehouse but will avoid expensive reads of input data.

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — a test run against zero rows proves nothing about full production data
distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — --empty limits refs and sources to zero rows, it does not run against real data
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — dbt does still execute the model SQL against the warehouse under --empty, just with no input rows

stem: A model's enforced contract declares `host_id` as `integer`. The model's SQL returns `host_id` computed as a string expression, and the columns are also selected in a different order than they appear in the YAML contract. Which of these two discrepancies will actually cause the preflight check to fail?

option_texts.A: Only the column order mismatch on `host_id`; data types are inferred at preflight check time regardless of what the contract declares
option_texts.B: Only the data type mismatch on `host_id`; the preflight check is agnostic to column order
option_texts.C: Both discrepancies independently fail the build, since dbt requires exact order as well as exact types
option_texts.D: Neither `host_id` discrepancy fails the preflight check, since contracts only check that every declared column name is present

drill_answer_short: A data_type mismatch fails the preflight check; column order does not matter to it
decision_hinge: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns with names and data types matching the ones you have defined. This check is agnostic to the order of columns specified in your model (SQL) or YAML spec.

plausible_options.C: the columns are also selected in a different order than they appear in the YAML contract

A.signal: The model's SQL returns `host_id` computed as a string expression
A.requires_fact: dbt will run a preflight check to ensure that the model's query will return a set of columns with names and data types matching the ones you have defined.

eliminated_by.D: The model's SQL returns `host_id` computed as a string expression

distractor_traps.A: T4: breaks a stated fact — the preflight check does compare data types, it is only order that it ignores
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — order is explicitly excluded from the check, so it is not a second, independent failure
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — names alone are not sufficient; declared data types are checked too
